extracted.intended_audience: policy makers, administrators, and scholars of unemployment insurance and administrative procedure (Canada-focused)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and organizational criteria for designing, operating, and reviewing the administrative decision-making process of a national unemployment insurance scheme (Canadian 1971 Act context). Includes institutional roles, decentralization, benefit eligibility/duration rules, financing, and procedural phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterisation as insurance (indemnify common risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scheme must indemnify (by means of cash benefits) the insureds (workers employed in insurable employment) against a risk which is common to all of them (interruption of earnings as a result of the termination of employment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This characterisation is not altered by requiring insured workers to pay premiums or by employers (non-insured parties) contributing; the central feature is the common risk of interrupted earnings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the covered risk — time-factor and continuous ascertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: The risk involves a state of affairs with an inherent time factor: the state of unemployment; unemployment insurance benefits are payable specifically while this state of affairs lasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the time factor the insurer must ascertain the existence of unemployment on a continuous basis rather than in a single operation; the administrative process must accommodate ongoing assessment of entitlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimant obligation — must not aggravate the risk; availability requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Under sec. 25 of the Act the claimant must be 'unable to obtain suitable employment', which assumes an attitude on his part conducive to obtaining one; the claimant may not, by his own actions, aggravate the risk assumed by the insurer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claimant's obligation consists of not prolonging the 'loss' voluntarily by adopting an attitude not conducive to obtaining suitable employment; procedural assessment must include evaluation of claimant behaviour/availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1971 Act expansion dimensions (four main areas)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1971 Act considerably enlarged the scheme in four main areas: the insured population, the financing arrangements, the range of benefits and the adjustment to the conditions of the labour market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four axes form the blueprint for substantive reform and must be considered when evaluating the scope and implementation of the scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insured population — near-universality by coverage expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Expansion to cover a whole range of jobs in the public and semi-public sector (public service, teaching, health services, armed forces and police) increased coverage from 80% to 96% of the working population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy design should consider inclusion of public/semi-public jobs to approach universal coverage; administrative capacity must scale accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financing arrangements tied to national unemployment rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Financing is based on the unemployment rate for the country as a whole: employers and employees bear the cost caused by a certain base level of unemployment (4% up to 1975; thereafter an eight-year average), with the federal government assuming responsibility for all costs in excess of that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Unemployment Insurance Commission must determine each year the proportion of expenses corresponding to the base level and the excess; budgeting and accounting procedures must support this allocation (cf. sec. 63 and 136).

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk-weighting (experience rating) for employer contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act provided for a system of risk weighting which would increase the proportion borne by employers relative to contributors as a whole based on degree of job stability within a company (firms with frequent layoffs pay higher premiums).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although present in the Act (sec. 64), implementation is optional and had not been implemented by the Commission at the time of writing; administrative systems must be prepared to calculate company-level risk weights if enacted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadened range of benefits with jurisdictional constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Special benefits for sickness, pregnancy and retirement were introduced in addition to regular unemployment benefits, but payment of such compensation must be linked to a state of unemployment to remain within federal legislative jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjustment of entitlement definitions was necessary to include claimants unable to work because of illness contracted after job loss or pregnancy (cf. secs. 25, 29, 30); legal alignment with constitutional powers must guide benefit design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefit-duration adjustment to labour-market conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Linking the period during which benefits are payable to national and regional labour market conditions: initial benefit period determined by weeks worked (18–29 weeks), with payable weeks between 8 and 15 depending on insurable employment; re-established initial benefit period of 10 weeks; extended benefit periods and automatic extensions tied to national/regional unemployment thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensions: claimants with >20 weeks insurable employment: 2–18 week extension; national unemployment >4% → +4 weeks; >5% → +8 weeks; regional adjustments where regional unemployment >4% and >1% above national can grant up to 18 weeks (cf. secs. 20, 32, 34, 37). Procedures must operationalize these conditional extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of procedural regularity given fiscal scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural regularity is essential because of the financial burden of the scheme on the public purse — amounts paid in benefits are large and growing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High financial stakes and large claimant populations require robust procedures, auditability, and controls; cyclical demand (e.g., winter peak) creates heavy pressure on claim processing that administrative planning must address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three essential elements required for a social security scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: A social security scheme providing cash benefits presupposes: (1) an administrative organization responsible for deciding each case; (2) dissemination among eligible population of information about the scheme and how to gain access; and (3) procedural machinery to enable individuals to gain access and claim benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program design and evaluation should check that all three elements are present and functioning (organization, outreach/information, access procedures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two logical phases of the procedure (formulation/implementation and review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure stages are grouped in two logical phases: the first comprises formulation and implementation of the decision by the administrative authority (positive in nature); the second comprises intervention (usually at request of public) of other normative agencies to review the initial administrative decision (critical in nature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of procedural fairness must consider both the administration's decision processes and the availability/effectiveness of review mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronological distinction within decision-making: preliminaries, decision, aftermath
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision-making process itself has a chronological distinction between the preliminaries of the decision (Chapter 1), the decision proper (Chapter 2), and its aftermath (Chapter 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural design and audits should examine each stage for adequacy: intake and preparation; decision-making standards and documentation; post-decision actions (notifications, enforcement, benefit control).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of responsibilities within internal administrative organisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal organisation contains allocation of responsibility between constituent units; the form will vary with decentralization and affects how the authority implements procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of procedural quality should map responsibilities (headquarters vs regional vs district vs local) and evaluate coordination, supervision, and accountability mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headquarters (central administration) roles and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The central administration (head office) coordinates and supervises operations, develops operating procedures, manages the Unemployment Insurance Account, provides policy direction, support, advice and coordination; in principle it does not intervene in individual claims decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headquarters must provide clear operating procedures and technical support while respecting delegated decision-making at decentralized levels; Operational Planning Branch intervenes in advisory capacity when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and appointment rules for Unemployment Insurance Commissioners
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission proper is composed of three Commissioners (one Chairman). Chairman holds office for 10 years, Commissioners for 5. For two Commissioners consultation must occur prior to appointment with 'organizations representative of workers' and 'organizations representative of employers'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tripartite representation aims to reflect participation of workers, employers and the federal treasury; Commissioners do not exercise judicial functions but influence procedure through regulation-making, internal minutes, and administrative direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and responsibilities of the Unemployment Insurance Advisory Committee
rubrics_metrics.description: Committee of 6–8 members appointed after consultation; duties include reviewing 'the state of the Unemployment Insurance Account, the premium rates, the adequacy of coverage and benefits' and any other matter relating to provision of unemployment insurance; may report annually or specially and may be directed to examine particular matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee is advisory only; Commission may refer matters directly to it for advice (in which case reporting is not required). Its opinions can inform procedural and policy adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decentralization principles: hierarchy of offices and service unit concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy of territorial decentralization is organized by (1) hierarchy of branch offices (Regional, District, Local) and (2) service unit concept applying to operations; decentralized units handle virtually the entire process of individual claim decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and evaluation must consider how decentralization affects uniformity, local styles, operational autonomy, and the capacity of service units to handle claims and maintain files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional Office functions and limits (payment centralization, technical supervision, exceptional decision involvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regional Offices perform technical services and supervise subordinate offices; issuance of benefit cheques and attendant data processing are centralized at regional level (Regional Payment Centre). Regional Offices normally do not make individual decisions, but may intervene in complex group claims (e.g., labour disputes) requiring uniform solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regional autonomy can create 'regional styles'; procedures must define the circumstances and processes for regional intervention in substantive decision-making and for ensuring consistency across districts.

rubrics_metrics.name: District Office as original jurisdiction for benefit decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The District Office holds 'original jurisdiction' with regard to benefits: this is the level where most decisions to grant, refuse or withdraw benefits are made; district opens and maintains each claimant's file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District internal organisation should include manager, Chief of Operations, service units responsible for decision-making, benefit control, administrative services, public relations, and labour market analysis. Evaluation should focus on staffing, file-keeping, and decision quality at this level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and functions of local office types
rubrics_metrics.description: There are seven different types of local offices classified by services they perform: Type 1 (District Office), Type IM (metropolitan variant), Type 2 (simplified District Office), Type 3A (service to claimants with one service unit and retained files), Type 3B (reduced staff, initial processing, no kept files), Type 4 (part-time visiting officers), Type 5 (minimal information service often located in Canada Manpower Centres).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of office type should match population density and service needs; whether claimant files are retained locally affects the locus of decision-making and early need for District Office intervention.
